sections.content: Despite the name "Calculus," this is essentially a rigorous mathematical analysis course. Topics include limits of sequences, properties of limits, monotone sequences, the Cauchy criterion, limits of functions, continuity, the Intermediate Value Theorem, and invertible continuous functions. Differentiation covers linear approximation, derivatives, monotone functions, extrema, the Mean Value Theorem, Taylor expansion, convex functions, graph sketching, and Newton's method. Expect heavy emphasis on logic and rigorous proof writing throughout.
sections.teaching: Ivan is genuinely excellent. He doesn't just copy-paste proofs onto slides — he walks you through the logic behind each step and builds intuition for why each theorem works. This makes even difficult analysis concepts much more approachable. Lecture notes and Zoom recordings are available after each class, which is a huge plus for review and catching up on anything you missed.
sections.grading: The exams are challenging, but the grading is fair and generous. The midterm mean was around 28 and the final mean around 42. If you score near the mean on both exams, expect a B to B+ range. So while the absolute scores may look low, the curve ensures reasonable outcomes for consistent effort.
sections.workload: The workload is heavy. Expect one problem set per week with around 10 questions, but don't underestimate them — each question is conceptually demanding and can easily take over an hour if your fundamentals aren't solid. Strong command of definitions and proof techniques is essential to keep up without burning out.

sections.content:
This lecture consist of many concepts for math genius. It touched the most fundamental part of math, which is like proving 1+1=2.

Chapter 1: limit (before mid-term):

We are first being introduced about some basic limit rules like sandwich or order rule, which should be easy for anyone who are confident in math.

Next we touched concepts like Axiom of Completeness, epsilon delta definition etc. These concepts are rigorous, even people who are confident with math would not be able to fully understand it. We are like computer engineer that type all the code using binary numbers instead of language like python or C++.

Chapter 2 derivative:
Less "rigorous" is included in this chapter, instead it becomes A level examination but much harder. Doing taylor expansion seems easy until you see a nested nested function in a limit. Calculations is the main point here which means students would generally perform better. However for students who never touched that much calculations before, you are going to get like 10 or 20 in final.
sections.teaching: Not much to say, average teaching. But he included a lot of meme in the lecture so I guess it makes the lecture quite interesting. But only math genius can follow through the lecture or else you better spend some time on the lecture recordings.
sections.grading: Pretty generous. Anyone that can understand all the concept would easily get B or above. But that is only true for genius. Even if you are confident with math, you might fail it, therefore the grading is unpredictable and harsh even though it is generous.

sections.content: The course content delivered by the professor is profoundly rigorous and intellectually stimulating, rooted in the fundamental logic of mathematics. He starts from the perspective of real number completeness, systematically deriving the entire framework of mathematical reasoning from its most basic principles. For students genuinely passionate about mathematics and pursuing in-depth academic exploration, this content is exceptionally high-quality—it builds a solid theoretical foundation that is invaluable for advanced studies or theoretical research. However, it is utterly unsuitable for students outside pure mathematics, such as those in physics, engineering, or business. The material is overly theoretical, offering little practical utility for applied fields; its value lies solely in deepening one’s understanding of mathematical fundamentals, making it irrelevant for anyone not aiming for a career in theoretical math.
sections.teaching: The professor’s teaching style is incredibly engaging and humorous, enhanced by his identity as an avid anime and manga enthusiast. His instructional methods are creative and memorable: for instance, one exam question playfully asked students to write the full names of Cauchy and Weierstrass, adding a lighthearted twist to rigorous mathematical learning. Additionally, his PPTs are designed with charming anime-style visuals, which make even abstract mathematical concepts more approachable and enjoyable. His lectures never feel tedious—he skillfully weaves humor and pop culture references into complex theories, keeping the class dynamic and maintaining students’ interest throughout. This unique blend of academic rigor and playful presentation makes his classes stand out as both informative and entertaining.
sections.grading: My experience with the course’s grading policy was extremely disappointing and unreasonable. Prior to enrolling, I heard rumors that the honors course had a generous A-range, supposedly up to 50%, which motivated me to sign up eagerly. However, after the midterm exam, the reality proved drastically different: out of 200 students, only 23 received an A+. For everyone else, grades started directly from B and declined downward, with no A- or A grades awarded between B and A+. This policy is absurdly rigid and unfair. I ranked 29th in the class, just a few points shy of the 23rd place cutoff, yet I was only given a B. Such a harsh and inflexible grading scale fails to recognize the nuanced differences in performance among students, making the initial claim of a "large A-range" misleading and frustrating.
sections.workload: The workload for this course is overwhelmingly heavy—far exceeding the combined workload of my other four courses, even by several times. The problem sets are extremely intellectually demanding, requiring hours of intense critical thinking and problem-solving that often feel mentally exhausting. Exams are equally challenging, designed to test not just basic understanding but also the ability to apply deep theoretical knowledge to highly complex scenarios. I frequently found myself spending entire weekends and late nights working on assignments and preparing for exams, sacrificing time that could have been allocated to other courses or personal pursuits. For students already balancing multiple demanding classes, this excessive workload becomes unsustainable, making the course a significant source of stress rather than a fulfilling learning experience.

Usually ppl would use homework to “pull” the total score upwards.

Finally, generative AI is permitted in homework, but don’t expect it to be very useful, as the current AI technology has not been developed well enough to carry out consistent and accurate mathematical proofs. If you decided to find AI for assistance, make sure to check the response meticulously so as to ensure there are no logical errors. Although the AI may sometimes give correct answers, it may not be the “best” answer (eg correct approach but too many steps). Personally I found Deepseek and Grok give the most consistent answers. Make sure to enable the advanced thinking modes for the gen AI, or it’ll give logically incorrect responses for sure.

sections.content:
The course starts off with a rigorous introduction to limits(Chapter 1 and 2)

In chapter 1 it is the limit of sequences.
In chapter 2 it is the limit and continuity of functions, taught together in close conjunction with the idea of constant approximations.

Then the topic changes to differentiation on chapter 3. It not only simply mentions something like the derivative taught in high school calculus. It actually builds a close connection between concepts like linear approximation, differentiability and derivatives together with some rigor introduction to technical aspects.

On chapter 4 it jumps to high-order differentiation and the idea of polynomial approximations. At this stage one begins to recognize that there are actually many subtle differences between differentiability, approximations, and derivatives.

sections.content:
A good and satisfying course, for those potential math major students.
Covering:
   sequences (chapter one）
   functions  (chapter two)
   differentiations (chapter three)
Each chapter provides relevant propositions/rules and their proofs. As expected, we learn some fundamental knowledge about these stuffs, and how to use them to deal with math problem. Especially, seems that the understanding of different axioms/rules/propositions and their relationships is the core of this course, for instance, you need to learn how Lagrange Remainder theorem is proved---its proofs bases on several propositions proved in previous lectures, with each of them pointing to some earlier propositions(sounds like a recursion tree). Anyway, it aim is building the foundation for you upcoming math studys, so what you can expect is something fundamental, which is usually related to proof-based problems.
sections.teaching:
Actually, I think it might not be appropriate for me to make any comments on professor Fong's teaching, since most of the content I've learned is self-taught. However, there is one thing I can say: his lecture note helps me a lot. Organized beautifully with interesting problems followed behind each chapter, it absolutely worth reading through. As for lectures, I think he mainly focuses on propositions and its proofs. Seldom(?) does he talk about any problems provided in HW or lecture notes, but I suppose there is no need to---solutions are provided by students  in "discussions" in Canvas. But beware---these solutions are not always correct, so read it carefully.

By the way, I LOVE LIU WENWEI. His tutorial lessons is AWSOME!!!

Very nice content.
Professor Fong has exceptionally good lecture notes, which have a natural flow, making the content easy to understand. Lecture notes also include very good exercises, which I strongly recommend doing. I wish all the honors math courses had similar notes (and unfortunately, they don't).

Each assignment, called a problem set, contains around five nice problems, which are very similar to exercises in the lecture notes. There were 10 assignments.

Exams, however, are much more difficult than exercises in the lecture notes, so it is recommended to solve problems from past papers of prof. Fong and prof. Ivan Ip, which are approximately the same difficulty as the exam.

Overall, the course is very well-crafted to both provide you with a good amount of knowledge and improve your problem-solving skills. My friends, who did not do many proofs in high school said that the course significantly enhanced their proof skills.

sections.teaching:
----------------------------- 𝐋𝐄𝐂𝐓𝐔𝐑𝐄𝐒 -----------------------------

The teaching is very concise and clear, but the speed is very fast. His English accent is good enough for us to follow, and he knows Cantonese as well. You are free to ask him questions after the lecture. There is usually a 5 min break in the middle of a lecture, so your brain can take a rest.

The handwriting is done on GoodNotes with screen recording. If you cannot follow the pace, you can review the lecture by watching the video.

The course content follows mainly Yan Min's notes, but occasionally there will be extra content with supplementary notes. Besides, there will be 1 worksheet per 1-2 lessons that demonstrates some approaches to easier problems.

---------------------------- 𝐓𝐔𝐓𝐎𝐑𝐈𝐀𝐋𝐒 ----------------------------

There is 1 tutorial per week, demonstrating some approaches to very difficult problems, a lot with long solutions that won't appear in homework or exams. However, I think more explanation can be done on how the solutions are achieved, instead of leaving us the impression that only experienced math students can come up with the solutions.

------------------- 𝐅𝐈𝐍𝐀𝐋 𝐑𝐄𝐕𝐈𝐄𝐖 𝐒𝐄𝐒𝐒𝐈𝐎𝐍 -------------------

Before the final exam, there will be a final review session revisiting the concepts, demonstrating some problems, and going through the cheat sheet.
sections.grading:
------------------------------ 𝐆𝐑𝐀𝐃𝐈𝐍𝐆 ------------------------------

Take the maximum mark such that the total is 100%:

Homework 20%
Midterm 10%-40%
Final 40%-70%

This means you can save your midterm with your final, but not vice versa. Therefore, make sure you put enough effort into preparing for the final exam.

The grade is decent. A range is given to people with 60% total marks or above, though I was sadly 1.25 marks from A-. You secure a B+ if you are above the mean.

-------------------------- 𝐁𝐎𝐍𝐔𝐒 𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐒 --------------------------

The homework offers a bonus course point of 0.2 by submitting a LaTeX-generated .pdf file and the original .tex file instead of handwriting. Therefore, you can get a total of 2 total course marks (without the *20% for homework). I think it is worth the time to type LaTeX, as the 2 course marks may be saving you for a higher grade.

You can also earn a bonus course point of 0.2 by finding and reporting a typo in Yan Min's lecture notes, homework, or homework solutions, capped at 2 points. Yan Min's notes contain a decent amount of typos, especially in computation steps, but hard to find in my opinion since the notes are quite long. In contrast, I think typos are easier to be found in Ivan's homework solutions. Some easy ones are missing a "d/dx" and missing a limit symbol.

There was also 1 bonus mark given by simply asking a question for the review session.

With the highest possible bonus course points of 5, you can get one subgrade higher, so they are worth the time completely.

------------------------------- 𝐄𝐗𝐀𝐌𝐒 -------------------------------

The midterm and final exams are extremely difficult, you will feel like vomiting blood during the exams. The exams kick off with a very tricky question (What is the name of the mathematician in the portrait?) (What is the meaning of some weird notation?). Then, there are a few short questions, which are already quite difficult for normal people like me.

Then, they are followed by 2-3 computation questions which are where most people get points from. Each is worth around 10 points. For your reference, midterm has limit computations that require you to apply basic limit knowledge like sinx/x->1 as x->0 and Squeeze Theorem, while final has limit computations that require you to apply the Taylor series (very ugly and tedious). Do not use a calculator to estimate the limit as the value may be extremely large.

Afterward, there are 2 long problems with around 4 parts each. These are the most difficult questions that I usually don't know how to do. But by writing something, regardless of correctness, the lenient T.A.s may give at least 1 mark. You can write down the approach to a problem if you failed to work out the exact details, and you will usually get more than half of the marks.

------------------------ 𝐆𝐑𝐀𝐃𝐄 𝐑𝐄𝐋𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐄 ------------------------

Finally, the final exam result and letter grades are quickly released within 24 hours after the final exam, so don't check your result if you think it may affect your performance in other final exams.
sections.workload:
--------------------------- 𝐇𝐎𝐌𝐄𝐖𝐎𝐑𝐊 ---------------------------

As a student who got 5** in DSE Math Core and 5* in M2, the workload was like an 8-credit course. But given this is an honor course, I would give the workload a D.

There were a total of 10 homework. Each homework would be released each week, containing 4 compulsory long problems and 1 optional problem with 2-4 parts each. But the deadline was usually 2 weeks later, meaning there was a week of buffer in case you cannot finish it within the first week.

The homework problems require a lot of thinking. Therefore, it's better to form groups to work on the homework, as lots of times, you wouldn't be able to come up with a solution. Usually, the solution only takes not more than 5 steps, so if your unsuccessful attempt is overly complicated, you may be in the wrong direction.

It took me around 5 days to complete one homework at the beginning of the course, and it gradually reduced to 3 days per week as I got used to the rigorousness.

However, the homework was very rewarding, not only because they were intellectually stimulating, but compared to MATH 1013 difficulty, you can have a good grasp of the concepts and computations in the topic, but it was completely not enough for handling Ivan's exams.

-------------------------- 𝐁𝐎𝐍𝐔𝐒 𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐒 --------------------------

The homework offers a bonus course point of 0.2 by submitting a LaTeX-generated .pdf file and the original .tex file instead of handwriting. This also takes a lot of time, usually within 1 day. I recommend using the online platform Overleaf - https://overleaf.com for its good editor (e.g. highlight brackets, the drop-down list for commands) and auto-save function. If your eyesight is not that good, you can use Mathcha - https://mathcha.io as it is a live LaTeX editor, i.e. you can directly edit the preview of math expressions with LaTeX instead of typing LaTeX code and then compiling it for preview.

If you are a perfectionist, do not fixate on the beauty of LaTeX, make sure you put enough effort into other courses and balance time well while you take this beast.

sections.content:
As an Honors Course, the content of MATH 1023 is indeed very difficult and challenging. It differs a lot from the mathematics you learn in secondary school and requires you to spend a lot of effort on thinking and understanding. You would need to prove a lot of things rather than just calculating them and you need to make sure every step is justified.

Even though the course is hard, it is worth taking since you can learn the 'real' mathematics and train your mathematical maturity. If you want to do a Math major, taking this course (and spending efforts on it) will definitely help you in your future study.
sections.teaching: Ivan is a kind professor, his English is clear and easy to follow. The teaching is good and the pace is reasonable. Nonetheless, I would suggest you go through the material by yourself before the class since you wouldn't have much time to think in class. It helps you with a better understanding.
sections.grading:
If you want a good grade and have no intention to do a Math major, I would recommend you take 1013 instead. Otherwise, I think you should take this course, regardless of the grade.

For your reference: I am a local student and attained level 5* in M2, have no prior knowledge other than the materials covered in M2 but still get an A-. Don't be too pessimistic, even though there are a lot of talented students taking this course.
sections.workload:
1 assignment per week. There are around 10 questions in each assignment. The time taken to complete the assignment really depends on your mathematical intuition, you can complete 1 question in several minutes if you think in the right way and you may also get stuck on 1 question for a whole day otherwise.

Apart from that, there is 1 tutorial per week and the questions are also very hard, I would recommend those who take the course study the questions before the tutorial, otherwise, you can hardly catch up with what TA is talking about.

Moreover, you have to spend a lot of time to fully understand the materials taught in class since this course has a strong emphasis on concepts and logic, you need to know why rather than how. To be specific, when studying the examples, ask yourself what is the reasoning behind those solutions rather than just knowing how the question is solved.

Professor Ip also included some of his own supplementary notes with extra proofs.
Basically a combination of MATH1013, MATH2033(MATH2043?) without integration, and about half of MATH2001.

Professor Ip will go through the lecture notes and 12 worksheets with us during lectures, and the TA will go through the 13 tutorial worksheets in the tutorials.

The content is as interesting as the difficulty of this course. Instead of just knowing how to do limits, differentiation, and remember certain theorems (what taught in 1013), I can actually know the reasoning and proofs behind.
As a local DSE student with neither math competition experience nor self-learned everything, I did feel extreme pain switching from M2 style computation-based math to MATH 1023 style rigorousness. However, it is quite satisfying once you can understand the theorems reasonably well (Doesn't need A+ level understanding to feel this satisfaction), basically opening a new world to you and make you view mathematics differently.

Slight criticism though:
The amount of content and level of difficulty (especially for Professor Ip's years) is a bit too much for a year 1 3-credit course.
sections.teaching:
Obviously, the instructor is Professor Ip, or Ivan.
The TAs are Hiu Chi Sit and Yunhe Li.

There are 2 80 minutes lecture and 1 50 minutes tutorial per week.
There will be an extra final review session.
Attendence will not be taken and lecture recordings will be uploaded to Canvas immediately after the lecture, so feel free to skip a lesson if you are sick.
Professor Ip also opened a class discord server for us, so he can release information, discuss math, or even chat casually there.
Note that I attended all lectures and tutorials.

Professor Ip is a good teacher.
His voice is moderately loud and his tone is quite chill. His English is quite good and the accent is very audible. He handwrites notes using a digital note-taking application as he speaks, and his font is acceptable.
He is well prepared before he comes to class and knows the content well, and explanation of content is quite clear. Even if he made a mistake, he will make corrections as soon as possible.
His teaching speed is quite fast, but is still acceptable to me.
He often includes jokes and easter eggs (eg. uses anime scenes as his Zoom virtual background) suring lectures and in homework/ exams.
If you do not understand, Professor Ip welcomes anyone to ask questions after the lesson, he will explain all of them clearly (except for the time he rushed to the cinema to watch One Piece Film Red). You can also ask questions on the discord server, as Professor Ip replies very quickly (at most within few hours).
Bonus: As Professor Ip is also a musician, he often invites us to attend his concerts.
Bonus 2: If you want to, he also doesn't mind eating lunch/ dinner with his students. Feel free to invite him to LG7 and chat casually with him on math, music and ACG stuff.

My TA was Hiu Chi Sit, so I cannot comment on Yunhe Li.

Hiu Chi Sit is a good TA.
Sadly, as he is always very sleepy, his voice lacks energy and may be hypnotizing to some people (not to me though). His English is good, and the accent is very audible.
He handwrites notes using a digital note-taking application as he speaks, yet his font is slightly unclear but still readable.
Hiu Chi Sit can explain the tutorial questions quite clearly.
However, he also have the problem of teaching a bit too fast.
If you have questions, you can raise them anytime, and he do not mind answering them. And if you have a lot of problems, he will answer most of them (before he gets too tired) as he marks homework in the library/ LIFS common.
He is also a very caring TA, as he encouraged me to move forward and not compare with others after I told him I fried my mid term.
sections.grading:
Grading is very very good.

The grading scheme is as follows:
Homework: 20%
Midterm: 10-40%
Final: 40-70%
(Take the maximum of the weights)
Bonus overall course points will be given if:
You reported math related typos in notes, worksheets, or homework (0.2 points per typo, 2 points maximum).
You typed your homework using LaTex (0.2 points per homework, 2 points maximum).
You submitted a question in the final review session (1 points maximum).

Note that Professor Ip and the TAs mark our homework and exam quite leniently, you get a lot of partial credits even if you can't do half of the question.

Professor Ip adopts a partially-absolute grading system.
The mid term, final, and overall grade books are attached below, so I won't mention the grades too in-depth here.
For this semester's case, in short:
Overall score of 60% or above can get A-range
Overall score of 39.71% or above can get B-range
Overall score of 20% or above can get a passing grade.
(Mean overall score is at 52.78%, i.e. B+)
As you can see, the A-range and B-range are very wide.

I expected a B+ or maybe even B from the start, but still managed to get an A- even though I was below mean in the mid term. I was very surprised when I checked my grades, and I kind of think that I do not deserve an A- (please don't take it back though). I am truly grateful for Professor Ip's generosity.
sections.workload:
Workload is very heavy (to me).

There are 1 homework with 4 long questions (and an ungraded bonus question) almost weekly, and the deadlines are set 2 weeks after release.
In total, there are 10 homework.
The homework questions are mostly quite hard, so be prepared to spend a lot of time on them.
In fact, I spent most of my time on MATH1023.
Also, it is not a shame to work with your peers, so please ask your friends for help if you do not know how to do your homework.
As you do your homework, you most likely need to review the course contents, so it that you effectively studied a few times as you do your homework, but it is very time consuming.
Please be reminded that the bonus questions are usually very hard, sometimes even those who got A or above cannot solve them, so do not be frustrated if you failed to do some of them, you are already very good.
Moreover, LaTex is brand new to me, and I spent quite a lot of extra time typing my homework using it.
At the beginning, I usually use about 6 days for each homework, and eventually the time decreased to 3 to 4 days when I got used to the contents.

Besides homework, you also need to spend a lot of time to understand the concepts.
Again, don't be afraid to ask your friends/ professor/ TAs for help. I can understand most of the concepts only because I have knowledgeble friends and kind professor and TAs.
It should take at least 4 or 5 days of studying before each exam.

I know that some may do extra exercise (eg. Rudin's textbook, HKALE, etc.), but homework and revision already took up most of my time, so I did not have time to find any.

This course will mess with your study schedule, sleep schedule, reduce your freetime, and give you depression (since your classmates are very strong) to some extent, depending on your ability.
I personally sacrificed a lot of sleep time to finish the homework.

To (hopefully) decrease your workload in your first fall semester, please study HKALE Pure Mathematics/ mathematical analysis as soon as possible. Although it may not help you solve Professor Ip's extra hard questions, prestudying can certainly help you understand the concepts more easily.
In case you are about to take this course, please kindly remind your cute 師弟師妹s, thankyou~

sections.content:
Limit: limit of sequence, properties of limit, monotone sequence, Cauchy criterion, infinity, limit of function, continuous function, intermediate value theorem, invertible continuous function

Differentiation: linear approximation, derivative, properties of derivative, monotone function, extrema, means value theorem, high order approximation, high order derivative, Taylor expansion, convex function, sketch of graph, Newton's method

This course focuses greatly on conceptual understanding. Because of this, you avoid tedious calculations.

While this looks like a regular calculus course, it's actually an intro to math analysis in disguise. Check Ivan's meme below :P Everything is proven rigorously from the ground up.

I absolutely recommend enrolling in this course if you enjoy math, even if you're taking a different major.
sections.teaching:
Best prof!!!

Ivan is always well-prepared, so the lessons are organized very logically. While he generally bases his lectures on Yan Min's lecture notes, he sometimes rearranges certain parts to make the flow of ideas easier to understand.

He is also very engaging. He'll give time to ask questions whenever dealing with difficult concepts.

The pacing is very good. To maximize results though, it's best to go through the lesson beforehand, so you won't get lost. Additionally, there's a mid-class break, which is very nice.

While each has only 4 problems, you'll probably need to allot around 10 hours per homework if you really want to learn the lesson well. I think this workload is (sort of) expected since this is an honors course. Rest assured, you'll learn a lot from them.

It may prove difficult to study for the midterm and final since they test a wide variety of techniques. You may understand the concepts but still fail if you don't practice enough. Unless you're a genius, then just like Ivan, you'll find them trivial. Otherwise, I suggest you put in the time necessary to practice all sorts of problems related to the lessons learned.

Course Description:
"This is the first in the sequence MATH 1023 – MATH 1024 of honors courses in one-variable calculus, with strong emphasis on rigorous mathematical reasoning.

This course will cover limit and differentiation.

Limit: limit of sequence, properties of limit, monotone sequence, Cauchy criterion, infinity, limit of function, continuous function, intermediate value theorem, invertible continuous function

Differentiation: linear approximation, derivative, properties of derivative, monotone function, extrema, means value theorem, high order approximation, high order derivative, Taylor expansion, convex function, sketch of graph, Newton's method"

As mentioned, this course focuses on Limits and Differentiation (Integration and Series will be done in MATH1024). What's special about this course is that it emphasizes on mathematical rigor, i.e. every statement should be precisely defined or logically sound (up to some assumptions); which means the MATH1023 will focus on these points:
· Motivation + Observations
· Conceptual Understanding
· Logical Definitions
· Theorems (+Proofs)
· Examples & Applications.

And as you can see, it is very different than MATH1012 or 1013 since they are both mostly focused on computations,which is why the course is highly recommended to those who are planning to do a maths major (specifically pure maths) or even doing theoretical physics.

This course is very different than school maths because it exposes you to the world of proofs and conceptual understanding of math, but it gives you a great learning experience that you won't find in any other course.

sections.content:
1. Intuitive Limit of Sequences
2. Rigorous Limit of Sequences
3. Monotone bounded and Cauchy Sequences
4. Limits of Functions
5. Continuity
6. Intermediate Value Theorem
7. Mean Value Theorem
8. Derivatives
9. L'Hopital's Rule
10. Taylor Series
11. Lagrange Remainder Theorem

There were also other things that FF added in to his pleasure, such as little-o notation, linear approximation, Cauchy mean value theorem, and some supplementary proofs for different theorems.

For those who want to take this course, I strongly recommend you self-study some HKALE Pure Maths. Although the content of this course is beyond the scope of HKALE Pure Maths, it is better to expose yourself to those concepts first, other than diving into them rigorously straight on. Moreover, some HKALE Pure Maths concepts are treated as trivial, and used often, such as the AM-GM inequality, triangle inequality, and various algebraic manipulation skills.

I got a 5* in 2020 HKDSE M2, and I can assure you that M2 is absolutely useless as a prerequisite. This course focuses more on proofs than computation. Instead of finding the limit, you need to prove the limit exists, which is completely different.
sections.teaching: FF tries very hard to ensure that everyone understands what he is talking about, and answers questions as comprehensively as he can. Of course, due to the nature of this course, "trivial" steps to solution are sometimes left out. FF's lectures are enjoyable, and he sometimes cracks out a few awkward jokes, pressuring us to laugh. I only missed 3 lectures. Moreover, FF is very close to students, as he even organizes "extra-curricular activities" for students to join.
sections.grading:
Extremely beautiful grade.

HW: 394/450
MT: 48/100
FL: 63/100
Bonus: 2.25/3
Overall Grade: B+

To prepare for exams, redoing your homework problems is the best. I didn't touch any exercises on the suggested textbooks FF provided, and only redid the homework.

To be honest, I think it is impossible for anyone who hadn't learnt the content of 1023 already to get A range (or at least learnt HKALE Pure Maths). Switching from "unrigorous" maths to rigorous maths is a mind-blowing experience.
sections.workload:
One problem set would be given every 1.5 weeks on average, depending on the mood of FF. Each problem set contains 3 to 6 questions, also depending on the mood of FF. There are a total of 9 "compulsory" homework (not really compulsory, since you can choose for the weighting of homework to be 0%), and 1 bonus homework. Bonus marks are given for those homework submitted with Latex.

Sometimes, FF adds contemporary unsolved mathematical challenges into the homework, hoping some prodigy would solve it. Other times, FF may pull inspiration from his own published papers or HKALE past paper questions.

Truth be told, the homework are fun to solve, but not fun to do (I never thought Intermediate Value Theorem could be so hard). But overall, the homework helps me understand what the heck is going. As a deadline fighter, I would finish the homework at the day the homework was due.

You can team up with other people for the homework, with at most 3 people I think, and your team would share the homework score. Be sure to find a teammate who is good at real analysis. FF may spare you some hints if you ask him kindly enough (or annoy him with sufficient tenacity).

λ ∈ [0, 20%], μ ∈ [0, 40%], ν ∈ [40%, 70%], λ + μ + ν = 100%}.

I assume this column is in fact asking what effort is needed to get a good grade. I'd directly quote what the Prof said.

Study Tips for MATH 1023

Rule of Thumb for all university MATH courses (not just 1023)

Put continuous effort in the course throughout the semester! Understand all fundamental concepts by regularly attending lectures, reading lecture notes, and discussing with teaching staff and classmates. Develop your mathematical maturity and problem-solving skills through exercises and homework. Don't expect you can skip all lectures or exercises, and then "爆seed" by intensive/overnight revision the day before the exams! It is impossible to absorb all course materials in just one night.

(see the meaning of "爆seed" here (Links to an external site.)Links to an external site.)

Be critical

Don't just learn math superficially by memorizing formulae or by following homework solutions blindly. University level math, especially this honor course, emphasizes much more on logical thinking than high school math. Always ask for the reasons and make sure you are able to justify every step. Don't feel satisfied by just asking "how", but ask also "why", "what if", "under what conditions", "what's good", etc. To get started, you should first change the mindset that learning math is not about memorizing or doing routine calculations.

Be logical

When you learn a theorem, don't just look at the "formula part". It is more important to keep in mind the necessary conditions and hypotheses in order to apply those theorem. For instance, look at the statement:
LaTeX: \displaystyle\text{If } \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \text { and } \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M, \text{ then } \lim_{x \to a} f(x) + g(x) = L + M. If  lim x → a   f ( x ) = L  and  lim x → a   g ( x ) = M ,  then  lim x → a   f ( x ) + g ( x ) = L + M .  
Many high school students would just memorize the rule that:
LaTeX: \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to a} f(x) + g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) + \lim_{x \to a}g(x)} lim x → a   f ( x ) + g ( x ) = lim x → a   f ( x ) + lim x → a   g ( x )   
but ignore the assumption that both LaTeX: \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \text{ and } \lim_{x \to a} g(x) lim x → a   f ( x )  and  lim x → a   g ( x )   have to exist (and finite) in order to make use of this rule.

In this course, you should always pay attention to the assumptions and conditions of a theorem. Ask yourself whether the theorem would fail if these conditions are not met. Furthermore, such a condition or assumption must be used somewhere in the proof, ask yourself where this condition appears in the proof and why it is needed!

Be a good listener

While my lectures will be based on the lecture notes, they are not merely the "audio" version of the notes. By just reading the lecture notes, you may only learn how to do math, but in lectures/tutorials you will learn why math is done that way, and in the long-run you will also learn the way of thinking of the instructor and TAs. Therefore, try to focus on listening and thinking during class. Taking notes (blindly) may hinder your thoughts. All blackboard notes written during a lecture will be recorded in a PDF that you can check it up later.

Work smart (not just work hard)

Learning mathematics -- just like learning "九陰真經" -- requires intensive practicing, deciphering, but not just passively by quick reading (though mathematics is not like "葵花寶典" that you need to "sacrifice" in order to learn it). Do relevant exercises soon after a lecture. Work hard and do more exercises than assigned; but work smart -- don't just do exercises of the same type over and over again. After you feel confident with basic and routine problems, go deeper on more structured and thought-provoking problems to broaden your knowledge and skills. Don't just do ALL exercises in ONE book, but do SOME exercises in SEVERAL books. Kenneth Ross's book on Elementary Analysis is a good one. Some structured problems of the deceased HKALE Pure Math were very well written -- that you can learn something new in a "guided" way.

Learn from people

Math is not fun if you learn it alone. Form a small group (such as with your highschool-mates, o'camp group-mates) to study the course together. Whenever you find difficulty in a homework problem, discuss it with your friends first to exchange ideas. If the problem is still not resolved, ask instructors and TAs for hint. If you are afraid of finding the instructor and TAs alone, go together with your group.

sections.content:
Before midterm:(Rigorous) definition of limit of sequence, sandwich theorem, monotone convergence theorem, Cauchy Sequence, (rigorous) definition of function limits

After midterm: Continuity, IVT; Differentiation, linear approximation, implicit differentiation, MVT, L'Hopital's Rule, taylor series, higher derivative test, concavity and Jensen's Inequality.

    (Almost) Everything is derived from scratch so no prior knowledge is needed (in the sense that it won't help), but mathematical maturity is a must, and you will definitely develop that from homeworks and tutorials.

    This course really encourages thinking the logic and proof behind everything instead of doing boring computations (we do have some though).  We started by assuming only the most basic rules (like arithmetic rule of limits), and then use the rigorous definition to build up everything. It makes you think twice on any seemingly easy question, and think of what you actually did, instead of skipping steps all over like what I did in DSE.

    I had a friend asking me about a limit problem and I explained to him the arithmetic rule, and the composition rule, and he don't understand. He said: What are all those rules? I didn't use those rules and I got the answer anyways. I said: You said you didn't use it because you don't know you are using it. That's why you get things wrong. You just assumes things and blindly use it (like the L'Hopital's Rule). Taking MATH 1023 really made me more careful when doing problems.

    (Some contents actually overlap with MATH 2033 so if you have made your way to the end of 1023, you should have an easier time in that. Professor said that some of our content is actually harder.)
sections.teaching:
His teaching is good. He often make jokes in lectures which helped (at least) me focus. We often have breaks in between so we can digest what he just said and we can ask questions as well.

    One time he devoted the whole lecture talking about the application of IVT, albeit not quite related to the course, is definitely interesting if you like maths.

    Keep in mind that the homework is much more difficult than the lectures, and professor said that the learning really only begins in the homework.

    The tutorials are ok. Sometimes the TA prepared some questions that he have no idea how to solve, or need to use clueless complicated stuff to solve. And he sometimes can't finish the notes. There are good questions in the tutorial though.

(Almost) Every Thursday and Friday night I would be just hating my life, but finishing those questions give you that sense of satisfaction and joy (that's right) when you finally think of the trick needed, or done the question, that MATH 1003/1012/1013 would never be able to give you. Until next week and the cycle continues.

    If you want to pwn this course, what are you smoking? But if you really do, you really need to spend time into not only the homework, but also the problems in Prof. Yan's notes, which would help you clear your concepts and learn some tricks, and extra exercise from other references.

    If you think that you can overcome the homework (don't overlook their difficulty and time required!), then definitely take this course. You will not regret it.

    Oh and by the way, the midterms and finals are open-notes and you can bring 2 notebooks, and you can use a calculator as well! Not that any of that are useful, but hey. Copy down all homework solutions ( and digest them) and you will be set for both.

sections.content: Before the midterm, the course covers the rigorous definition of limits (That is how to prove for example that the limit as x approaches a of x^2 = a^2 using well defined mathematical formulations and being rigorous while doing so). This part emphasized proofs and professor Hu Proved everything he wrote, and I mean everything. You won't be expected to repeat his proofs in the exam but you are expected to understand them since you can use a similar way to prove other questions he might ask. Also, he covers all the differentiation rules and again proofs the product rule, quotient rule, etc. After the midterm, he focused on on the applications such as optimization problems, sketching graphs, intermediate value theorem, mean value theorem, L'hospital rule, local and global minima and maxima, concavity, etc. Overall, the course has a really rewarding content and I definitely recommend taking it if 1) you don't care about the grade that much and 2) if you are going to major in maths. The course has improved my mathematical maturity so much and made me think of most stuff in terms of their proofs and definitions, definitely a well constructed calculus course and is almost the same difficulty (if not harder) than other calculus courses in other US universities such as MIT and Caltech, etc.
sections.teaching:
Professor Hu, for me is one of the best mathematics professors that ever thaught me in my life. He has many famous sentences such as: "You don't know the definition, you get a big 0" and "Your intuition tells you that this limit is 0? well my intuition tells me that YOU get a 0" and finally "Analysis is a hard subject, every year at least 3 people commit suicide in MIT because of analysis:". Professor Hu teaching is extremely funny and laid down and you can sense he enjoys what he does, he focuses on two things: LOGIC and DEFINITION, if you lack one in your answer then you're getting a big 0. For example, the limit as x approaches infinity of (1/(x+4)) = 0 since the denominator grows to infinity and 1 divided by a very big number is 0. if you write this in the exam you get a 0. To get the mark, you can either 1) proof that the limit of 1/x+4 is indeed 0 by the DEFINITION or use logic and algebraic manipulation to write 1/x+4 as (1/x)/(1+4/x). since we know limit as x approaches infinity of 1/x = limit of 4/x  = 0 and by the continuity of the polynomials, the limit is 0/(1+0) = 0/1 = 0 therefore we conclude the limit is 0. See how many steps we needed to show the limit of such an easy limit is 0? you have to follow similar arguments in ALL your answers or else, a big 0.

A final word about the TA (Xilin Li), this is arguably one of the best TAs in the maths department, the guy is very nice, he explains things thoroughly and you can meet him after class and he would even explain FULL lessons to you after class if you need it, he is always at the maths support center most of the time and I honestly wouldn't have gotten my A- without this guy. Seriously a life saver.

Also, for the lecture notes, review the attachments below, study from these notes since they are much harder and rigorous than the Stewart calculus book. everyone studies from it.
sections.grading:
The grading is shit, no way to put it except this way. The students who take this course are all really mathematically mature and well, really really good in maths. When I went to professor Hu at the beginning of the year, I asked him if I should take the course since I am an international student and most students who take it are from mainland (if not all of them) and they are known to be the best in maths. He told me you should take it butt you might get a C or C+ even if you're good because these guys are really good, I ended up in the end getting an A- (Even though I regard myself to be exceptional in mathematics and I ranked in the top 1.8 percentile in the maths exam in my country) and I studied a lot! So if this tells you something, its that the course is full of good people, and in the end, around 40% got A- or higher and I barely hit the A- level. So be very careful if you need to maintain a certain gpa for your scholarship, I know you might really think you are very good in maths, but so did I and you're going to have to work your ass off just to get an A.

45% midterm, 5% H.W, and 50% finals.

sections.teaching:
Very nice! Clearly he teaches with heart and brain. I don't know how to describe how well he taught. But I can assure you that his teaching could elevate your understanding in calculus to a whole new level.

What he focused on is DEFINITIONS! He said it many times in the lesson, 'MATHEMATICS IS ABOUT DEFINITIONS!!!!!' So instead of testing a hell ton of algebraic techniques he rather tested on how well you reason your steps. He once said it class while pointing his finger to a student, 'Your intuition tells the limit is 0, you get a 0!' I got a mark deduction because of skipping a tiny step when proving limits -.-!

But his approach of marking really forced students to beware of the importance of definitions, which makes 1023 much more rewarding (in terms of content only) than 1013. 1023 helps students adapting uni math. Students will eventually realize how dangerous it will be to do math without understanding definitions.
